meta.title: tmux in any browser, on any phone — one command, no SSH
meta.description: Run one command and the tmux sessions already on your machine open in any browser. Scan the QR to attach — end-to-end encrypted, nothing to port-forward.

hero.title: Your tmux sessions in any browser, <accent>even the one in your pocket</accent>.
hero.subhead: The same tmux server your laptop attaches to, open in a browser tab on your phone.
hero.answer: mtmux is a command-line tool that serves the tmux sessions already running on your machine to any web browser. Install it with <cmd>npm i -g mtmux</cmd>, run <cmd>mtmux</cmd>, and scan the QR code it prints: your phone attaches to the same tmux server over an end-to-end encrypted tunnel. No port forwarding, no VPN and <post>no SSH key on the phone</post>.

demo.title: One command, then close the laptop.
demo.description: mtmux runs next to your tmux server. Nothing is copied and nothing is synced — <post>your browser is just another client</post> attaching to the same session. Here is the whole thing, start to finish.

install.title: Install it
install.description: One global package. Node 22 and tmux are the only prerequisites.

pair.title: Run it
pair.description: It serves this machine's tmux and dials out to open a sealed tunnel, then prints a QR and a nine-digit code. No config file, nothing to forward, no account.

attach.title: You're attached
attach.description: <post>Real panes, real scrollback, real keys</post>. The six-digit half of the code never reaches our servers, and the browser is trusted from then on.

move.title: Move around
move.description: Swipe left or right to step through your tmux windows — and through the panes of a window when one is zoomed. The strip above the terminal always shows exactly what a swipe will step. Tap any tab to jump straight there.

agent.title: Close the tab
agent.description: The session never belonged to the browser. Whatever was running keeps running, and it is still there when you come back.

transport.reducedNote: Playback is turned off because your system is set to reduce motion. Use the numbered steps below to move between frames.

a11y.description: A replay of a terminal running mtmux beside a phone browser. The terminal installs mtmux, runs it, and prints a pairing code; the phone enters the code, attaches to the session, and swipes between three tmux windows.

fidelity.title: Real tmux. Not a screenshot of one.
fidelity.description: Every keystroke goes to the same pty your laptop talks to. Your config, your plugins, your keybinds — untouched.

features.title: A prefix key you can actually press
features.description: A sticky modifier row puts ⌃b, esc, tab, alt and the arrows one thumb away, so a chord is two taps instead of a contortion.

features.title: Panes that fit the screen you have
features.description: Reflow stacks a three-pane layout vertically on a phone and leaves the tmux window your desktop is attached to alone.

features.title: Truecolor and the glyphs you use
features.description: 24-bit colour, powerline separators, box drawing and Nerd Font icons render the way they do in your terminal emulator.

features.title: Scrollback with real search
features.description: Scroll back through a pane's history and search it, and copy-mode selections land in your device clipboard.

features.title: Survives the tunnel
features.description: The client reconnects on its own, so a dead spot in the subway costs you a moment rather than the session.

features.title: A file browser when you need one
features.description: Read a diff or a log without leaving the tab. Paths are allow-listed, so a paired browser only reaches what you let it.

agents.title: Check on the run without <accent>going back</accent>.
agents.description: <post>Long agent runs</post> are why most people want this. Claude Code, Codex or aider is thirty minutes into a refactor and you are not at the desk — so open the session on your phone and look at it.

points.title: The same pane, not a summary
points.body: You see exactly what the agent printed, because you are attached to the same pty. Nothing is parsed, sampled or reworded on the way to you.

points.title: Answer the prompt yourself
points.body: Agents stop on approval dialogs and y/n questions. From a phone that is one tap on the modifier row, and the keystroke goes straight to the pane.

points.title: Start the next one from the platform
points.body: Scrollback, search and a real prefix key mean you can read the diff, kick off the next task and get off the train.

points.title: Nothing to configure
points.body: mtmux does not watch your panes, match on output or try to guess what an agent is doing. It attaches to tmux, and that is the whole feature.

honest.label: to be clear
honest.body: mtmux <post>does not send notifications</post>. There is no push, no Slack routing and no agent detection. It is pull, not push — you open the session and look.

security.title: The relay cannot read your session.
security.description: Pairing is a PAKE, so the six secret digits never reach our broker — not even as a hash. Everything after that is sealed under keys nobody on the path can derive.

cells.title: End-to-end encrypted
cells.description: CPace over ristretto255 to pair, HKDF-SHA256 to derive keys, AES-256-GCM per frame. The broker moves ciphertext.

cells.title: Nothing to port-forward
cells.description: The CLI dials out. No firewall hole, no VPN, no dynamic DNS, no sshd facing the internet.

cells.title: Per-device revocation
cells.description: <cmd>mtmux devices revoke</cmd> forgets a browser's key by id, so it cannot reconnect.

cells.title: Or skip us entirely
cells.description: <cmd>mtmux start --local</cmd> contacts no broker at all, and <cmd>MTMUX_API_URL</cmd> points at your own.

openSource.title: MIT licensed. Run all of it yourself.
openSource.description: The CLI, the browser client, the relay and the pairing broker are one public repo under one MIT licence. There is a hosted broker because it is convenient, not because anything depends on it.

cli.title: The CLI is already self-hosted
cli.description: It runs on your machine, talks to your tmux, and holds its own token. Nothing is uploaded and no account is created. For one machine this is the whole answer.

local.title: Or contact no broker at all
local.description: <cmd>--local</cmd> serves your LAN and loopback and dials nothing — by choice, not by the tunnel quietly failing. Put your own reverse proxy in front of the single port and you are reachable from anywhere without us.

broker.title: Or run the pairing broker too
broker.description: The broker is in the same repo and is blind by construction — it never sees the secret half of a code, and it moves ciphertext it cannot open. Point the CLI at yours with <cmd>mtmux config set api</cmd>.

compose.title: your own broker, in four lines
compose.note: It comes up working with <cmd>DATABASE_URL</cmd> unset: no accounts, no billing, no secrets to manage, anonymous pairing on. Accounts are optional forever, and that is the default rather than a degraded mode.

pricing.description: Local and LAN traffic never touches our infrastructure, so it is never metered. Relayed bytes are the only thing that costs us anything, so they are the only thing we count.

items.question: Does mtmux replace tmux?
items.answer: No. It attaches to the tmux server you already run, the same way tmux attach does. Uninstall mtmux and every session keeps running.

items.question: Do I need to install an app, or an account?
items.answer: Neither. The client is a web app — open the URL the QR points at, or add it to your home screen for fullscreen keyboard handling. An account is optional and only buys you more than one registered server.

items.question: Does it notify me when my agent finishes?
items.answer: No, and we would rather say so than imply otherwise. mtmux has no notifications, no agent detection and no push. What it gives you is a session you can open from a phone in a couple of seconds and read.

items.question: Can my phone actually type in vim?
items.answer: For edits, yes — that is what the modifier row is for. Esc, ctrl, alt, tab and the arrows are always reachable and modifiers latch, so a chord is two taps. Writing a new module on a phone is still a bad idea.

items.question: Is the relay a man in the middle?
items.answer: It cannot be. The code splits into a routing half the broker sees and a secret half it never receives, and the session keys come out of a PAKE run between your machine and your browser. The broker forwards sealed frames and holds no key.

items.question: Do I have to use your servers at all?
items.answer: No. mtmux start --local serves your LAN and loopback and contacts no broker whatsoever. If you want the tunnel but not our broker, MTMUX_API_URL points the CLI at your own.

items.question: How is this different from tmate?
items.answer: tmate spins up a new session on its own relay so a guest can join you. mtmux attaches you to the tmux server you already run, from your own browser, and the secret half of the pairing code never reaches our broker. <post>The full comparison</post> covers where each one fits.
